When the consultation happened, and how far it stood from the act, is settled by two voices together. Gill places it at the gathering that made David king, noting on Lightfoot's authority that the thing advised was not done until considerably later, with Hiram's message, the taking of Jerusalem and two Philistine battles falling in between. Wesley gives the same sequence: the assembly was dismissed after the proposal was accepted, and only after the Philistines had been twice repulsed did David take up what he had resolved and call a second general assembly. Keil and Delitzsch set the chapter against its parallel instead. The facts are in the earlier history, mostly in the same words but differently arranged, because the author there weighed the transfer politically, as one of David's first acts towards raising the kingship, where the Chronicler has in view the religious significance of the design, the restoring of the Levitical worship prescribed in the law.

Henry supplies the reading of the consultation itself. David's two aims were to honour God by showing respect to the token of his presence, and to have the benefit of the oracle, so that those who honour God profit themselves. That he put the matter to the leaders at all, having authority to command it, Henry explains three ways: to show them respect, since no wise prince covets to be absolute; to be advised on the manner of doing it, because it is wisdom to use the wisdom of others; and so that the thing might pass as a national act. He notes two things in the address, that David calls the people brethren, which bespeaks humility in a man newly advanced, and that he speaks of them as a remnant left, their wars having wasted the country.

Who the congregation were is agreed. Gill makes them the officers as representatives, and both Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch put the number at the thirty thousand chosen men named in the parallel, Keil and Delitzsch adding that not all Israel can have been present but that there were representatives from every part. On the wording Ellicott is close. The condition is two independent clauses rather than one dependent on the other, if the thing be good before you and if the motion come from the Lord. The verb for sending means to break forth and so to send with all despatch, the word for land is plural, of the territories of the several tribes, and the Levites' cities are cities of their pastures, the Levites apparently following pastoral work when not engaged in religion.

The reason David gives for the removal turns on a phrase Ellicott will not take at face value. It should be rendered we sought it not, meaning neglected it, the ark having lain twenty years in Abinadab's house; and he suggests the suffix may refer to God rather than the ark, since there is no clear evidence that the ark itself was ever used as an oracle. Wesley fills in the neglect from the other side, that the people contented themselves with going to Gibeon to sacrifice and did not care that the ark, the soul of the tabernacle, was elsewhere. On the limits of the muster the two voices that give them disagree. Clarke reports the Targum, which runs the gathering from the Nile of Egypt to the entrance of Antioch. Ellicott identifies the southern boundary with the winter torrent now called Wady el Arish, while allowing that the same name elsewhere means the Nile, and takes Hamath for the standing name of the northern boundary and the seat of a kingdom independent of David but friendly to him, adding that interest in the place had revived with the discovery there of five undeciphered inscriptions pronounced Hittite.

Ellicott opens with a statement that governs his notes: from this point the narrative coincides with the older account, the original text being plainly the same whether the chronicler drew on that book or another source, the differences being abridgments, paraphrases and corrections. The town's older name was Baal's town, the other describing its wooded position, and here the text looks more correct than the parallel, where the word for lords may have swallowed the name. He also notes a habit running through the chapter, that where the older book writes the divine name the chronicler avoids it.

The procession is handled in a few pointed notes. Clarke explains the new cart as a precaution against profaning the ark by setting it on a carriage that had served common uses, and reports that all the versions and Jarchi take the second driver's name for brother or brothers, as Ellicott also allows. For the playing Ellicott gives dancing to music, and sets the words against the parallel, where a strange expression about woods of cypresses is probably a confusion of similar letters. On the clause about the Name the two voices arrive together by different routes. Clarke follows the Targum in reading that the name was not called upon the ark but invoked at it. Ellicott takes the Hebrew as it stands to mean who is called Name, since later Israelites substituted the Name for the divine name itself, but thinks a word meaning upon it has dropped out, giving the sense that the ark was called by the name of the Lord; manuscripts reading there instead of name yield Clarke's sense exactly.

At the threshing-floor the textual notes thicken. Ellicott prefers the parallel's form of the place-name, records that three versions render prepared threshing-floor, and calls the words about Uzza's hand an explanatory paraphrase of the older and barer text. On the reason given for the blow he is frank about the limits of the evidence: the older book has an obscure phrase found nowhere else, and whether the chronicler preserved the original reading or guessed at it cannot be determined. Henry draws six lessons from the death, of which the first two are the weightiest. Presumption, rashness and irreverence in holy things are to be feared, and no good intention justifies a bad action, so that in communion with God the heart must be watched lest familiarity breed contempt and we think God beholden to us. And the death proclaims a jealous God who will be sanctified in those that come near him, the nearer being the more exposed to displeasure for presuming; yet we may through Christ come boldly to the throne of grace.

Henry's remaining lessons bear on David rather than Uzza, and one of them is a criticism. The interrupted joy is a reminder to rejoice with trembling, and the king's displeasure a caution to watch our spirits under rebuke, since if God is angry with us we may not dare be angry with him. But the stopping of the whole business Henry will not excuse: David should have gone on with the work notwithstanding the breach, and so the breach might have been made up, providences of that kind being meant to drive us from our sins and not from our duty. Wesley carries both of those over almost word for word. On the house where the ark lodged, Clarke and Ellicott agree that Obed-edom was a Levite and only a sojourner at Gath, Ellicott adding that he belonged to the clan charged with carrying the ark. Clarke ends with the Targum's account of the blessing, that Obed-edom's wife and his eight daughters-in-law each bore eight at a birth, so that in one day fathers and children numbered eighty-one, and with his own dry verdict that the exposition will not be generally received, though rabbins must be allowed to deal in the marvellous.
